# Connect a third-party memory MCP server

English | [中文](mcp-memory.zh.md)

These three **default-off reference configurations** connect one memory system to DSH through [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client`](../../../packages/mcp/mcp-client/README.md). Pick one, or copy the same generic MCP row for another server.

These third-party configurations are provided as interoperability examples only. Their inclusion does not imply endorsement, recommendation, partnership, or ongoing support by DeepSeek.

## What DSH does

DSH parses the selected Cordis overlay, starts a configured stdio command or connects to a configured Streamable HTTP URL, discovers MCP tools, and exposes them as `mcp__<serverName>__<tool>`. DSH does **not** download the server, initialize its database, choose its model or embedding provider, create a cloud account, migrate vendor data, or supervise a separate HTTP service. For stdio, the generic client launches and stops the child with the DSH plugin lifecycle; for HTTP, the upstream service must already be running.

The stdio bridge deliberately removes ambient variables whose names usually identify credentials and all `DSH_*` variables before launching a child; other ambient variables remain inherited. Each example adds only the baseline override it needs. If an optional upstream feature needs another secret, add that variable to the row's `config.env` instead of putting the secret directly in YAML.

## Choose one

| System | Tested pin | Transport | Upstream prerequisite |
|---|---:|---|---|
| [Memorix](https://github.com/AVIDS2/memorix) | `memorix@1.3.0` (`500792cad3144142293bfbb20acb4841c9f7fcfa`) | stdio | Node 22.18+ and `npm install --global memorix@1.3.0` |
| [MCP Reference Memory](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/memory) | `@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@2026.7.4` (`6dd0a683e198783e30feabf7abaf42f925bd18b1`) | stdio | `npm install --global @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@2026.7.4` |
| [Engram](https://github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram) | `v1.20.0` (`ba9e46ced152c37a7cb9e576153c41995873e2fc`) | stdio | Go 1.25.10+ and `go install github.com/Gentleman-Programming/engram/cmd/engram@v1.20.0`, or the matching release binary |

## Enable one

Pass one overlay to DSH:

```sh
dsh web --patch "$PWD/apps/cli/config/examples/mcp-memory/memorix.cordis.yml"
```

overview: # Schedule reminders English | [中文](schedule.zh.md) ## Summary Ask the model in a conversation to create, list, view, edit, pause, resume, or delete reminders. Each reminder repeats by its rule and delivers its instruction to an existing conversation, to one new conversation, or to a new conversation at every occurrence. The Automation tasks page lists every reminder of the Host and can create, edit, run, pause, resume, and delete one. Delivered one-shot tasks remain available until you explicitly delete them. ## Table of Contents - [Create reminders](#create-reminders) - [Inspect, run, and delete tasks](#manage-tasks) - [Edit a task](#edit-timing) - [Timing and delivery reference](#timing-and-delivery) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) ## Create reminders The shipped Web profile includes the Host Schedule service and the Automation tasks page. Configure a model provider before asking it to create reminders. The `standard`, `cordis`, and `ptc` presets declare the four reminder tools and the clock context that gives the model the current time and the browser's zone, so those presets provide `schedule_create`, `schedule_list`, `schedule_view`, and `schedule_edit`; the `minimal` preset declares neither. A delegated subagent sees the four tools, but each tool refuses a call from a delegated subagent, so a subagent cannot read or change reminders. Ask the model to create, list, view, edit, pause, resume, or delete reminders. It uses `schedule_create` to create one, `schedule_list` to list the reminders of every conversation, `schedule_view` to read one, and `schedule_edit` to change, pause, resume, or delete one; an edit keeps the reminder id and saved delivery records. A reminder that the model creates has a name, an instruction, a start time in UTC or in an IANA time zone, and an RFC 5545 repeat rule, such as every weekday at 09:00 or only once. It delivers to this conversation, to one new conversation that its first delivery creates, or to a new conversation at every delivery; a new conversation uses the working directory and preset of this conversation. Each delivery of a reminder comes at least one minute after the scheduled time of the previous delivery, or after the previous Run now; a reminder that opens a new conversation at every delivery waits for the Host's minimum run interval instead, one minute by default. A late delivery, for example after a Host restart, does not delay the next one. A conversation that a delivery creates joins the Workspace registered at its working directory and takes the reminder name as its title. For a reminder that opens a new conversation at every delivery, the title also states the launch time in the zone of the reminder's rule, for example `Weekday digest · 2026-10-12 09:00`. For example, ask: “Remind me every day at 23:00 in Asia/Shanghai to check the weather.” Below the reply, a card shows the created reminder's name and frequency; Open shows its details in the right sidebar. Check that the frequency repeats every day at 23:00, not Once. A one-time reminder does not become recurring after delivery. After the reminder is deleted, the card shows Deleted and no longer opens it. To create a reminder without the model, open Automation tasks from the sidebar, open Choose a creation method beside New, and choose Create manually; when no task exists, New automation task opens the same editor. This editor also opens existing tasks and asks for an Automation task name, an Automation task instruction, Run in, Linked workspace, and Run time. It starts with Once at one hour from now in the browser's time zone and with Create a conversation and reuse it. Run in offers Create a conversation and reuse it, which creates one conversation at the first run and keeps using it, and New conversation for every run, which creates a separate conversation at each run and shows the Host's minimum run interval. Linked workspace lists each registered Workspace with its directory and selects the Workspace whose directory the new conversation uses; it starts at Default workspace, or at the first Workspace when the default Workspace is not registered. When no Workspace exists, Linked workspace shows Ungrouped and the Host project directory is used. The new conversation uses the default preset. Create creates the task and selects it in the list, and Discard closes the editor without creating one. If the Host refuses the task, the editor keeps your input and states the problem, for example that the date and time must be in the future.

overview: # Plugin indexes English | [中文](plugin-market.zh.md) ## Summary A plugin index is one JSON file that lists installable DSH bundles with their titles, icons, authors, and versions. Turn on the experimental **Custom plugin indexes** bundle to browse indexes in a **Discover** tab on the Plugins page and install a listed version after a confirmation. To publish an index, write or generate an index file and serve it, together with its icon files, from any static host. ## Table of Contents - [Turn on Discover](#turn-on) - [Browse and install](#browse-and-install) - [Publish an index](#publish-an-index) - [Generate an index with the reference generator](#generate-an-index) - [Index format reference](#index-format) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) ## Turn on Discover Open **Plugins**, find **Custom plugin indexes** under **Experimental plugins**, and switch it on. A **Discover** tab appears next to **Installed**, and Creator mode gains the read-only `plugin_market` tool. Switching the bundle off removes both again. DSH ships no index source. Select **Discover**, choose **Add index source**, and enter the URL of an index file. A URL must use `http:` or `https:` and must not contain a user name, password, or `#` fragment. Anyone on the network path can change an `http:` index, including the install specs it lists, so use `https:` for an index reached over a network you do not control. Each source belongs to the current profile. ## Browse and install The index menu at the left of the toolbar switches between sources and opens **Manage index sources…**, where each source shows its last error. Search matches names, authors, keywords, and titles, descriptions, categories, and labels in every language, and tolerates typos; results come in best-match order until you choose another. The **Labels** menu, category pills, and **Sort** menu use the categories, labels, and sort keys that the index declares, and **Publish date** sorts by each plugin's latest version. Each card shows the plugin's recommended version: the highest version compatible with the running DSH that is not a prerelease, or the highest compatible prerelease when the plugin lists no version without a prerelease tag. **Install** opens a confirmation with that version's source: the npm package and registry, or the Git repository, commit, and directory. Confirming starts the normal plugin installation, including its compatibility and registry checks; nothing is installed without that confirmation.

# Create review Sessions from GitHub webhooks

English | [中文](github-review.zh.md)

This opt-in overlay adds a signed GitHub endpoint to `dsh web`. When a pull request in the configured repository changes from draft to ready for review, the rule creates a titled root Session under the repository's Web Workspace and starts a read-only review prompt.

## Prerequisites

- A local checkout that DSH may register as a Web Workspace.
- A high-entropy GitHub webhook secret available through the `DSH_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` credential reference.
- A TLS reverse proxy or tunnel that can forward one public URL to the loopback listener.
- GitHub webhook subscription to the Pull requests event with content type `application/json`.

The overlay defaults the Workspace to the launch directory and the listener to `127.0.0.1:3081`. Override them with `DSH_GITHUB_REVIEW_WORKSPACE` and `DSH_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_PORT`.

## Start DSH

Generate a secret and retain the same value across restarts:

```sh
export DSH_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
printf '%s\n' "$DSH_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"
```

Install both experimental packages into the Web profile first. Profiles do not install peers automatically; the GitHub adapter needs the webhook runtime explicitly:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add @deepseek-ai/dsh-webhook @deepseek-ai/dsh-webhook-github
export DSH_GITHUB_REVIEW_WORKSPACE=/path/to/deepseek-harness
dsh web --patch "${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}/profiles/web/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/dsh-webhook-github/examples/github-review/cordis.yml"

overview: --- description: "Desktop runs the Harness workspace in a native application. This reference covers application behavior, development and integration; the packaging, Windows signing and publication guides own build and release operations." --- # DeepSeek Harness Desktop English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary Desktop runs the Harness workspace in a native application. This reference covers application behavior, development and integration; the packaging, Windows signing and publication guides own build and release operations. ## Table of Contents - [Application overview](#application-overview) - [Terminal command](#terminal-command) - [Closing the window and quitting](#closing-the-window-and-quitting) - [Key technical decisions](#key-technical-decisions) - [Bundled command runtime](#bundled-command-runtime) - [Installation ownership](#installation-ownership) - [Recovery and diagnostics](docs/diagnostics/README.md) - [Develop](#develop) - [Package](#package) - [Windows installer interface](#windows-installer-interface) - [Updates](#updates) - [Low-level development overrides](#low-level-development-overrides) - [Known limitations](#known-limitations) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ## Application overview Electron caches the last confirmed UI language in `userData/desktop/locale-cache` so startup recovery dialogs can use it before Host settings are available. Missing, invalid, or unreadable caches fall back to the system language; cache write failures do not block startup. A successful Host startup or a UI language change refreshes the cache. Until then, a changed system language may differ from the cached language. Desktop analytics follows the [product collection policy](../../packages/client/product-analytics/README.md), including its live application setting. Web usage is excluded. Update installation waits for its local analytics intake before locking API admission and stopping the Host. Intake has a one-second deadline; failure does not prevent installation, and collector delivery is not awaited. The desktop application is an Electron shell around the complete dsh Web application. An Electron RunAsNode child starts the shared profile runner, and Electron immediately loads the packaged Web entry at `dsh-app://app/`. Its shared loading page waits for Host boot injections, then starts the client without navigating to another document. Electron forwards application HTTP requests to the authenticated Web Host, dropping connection-level response headers (`transfer-encoding`, `connection`, `keep-alive`) that describe the Node fetch rather than the resource, and marking plugin bundle responses `no-store` because their per-launch revisions would only accumulate in Chromium's disk cache; WebSocket streams connect to that Host with credentials attached only for the owned application window. Node IPC carries boot injections, readiness, and shutdown. Desktop listens on an OS-assigned port by default, so it cannot collide with Web’s `3080` or a reserved port; a `webserver.config.port` patch can override it. Native Host requests send the current Host's authentication cookie explicitly, and no Electron session stores it; each Host start removes `dsh-auth-*` cookies that earlier releases left in the default session, because cookies ignore ports and would otherwise accompany every request to `127.0.0.1`. Desktop binds `127.0.0.1`, the address Electron dials for the ready URL and the WebSocket credential filter. WebSocket streams use `ws:` or `wss:` according to the Host listener; credentials require matching authority and scheme. The first application-menu command, **About DeepSeek Harness**, opens Electron's native About panel with the application icon, product name, and installed release version. The menu follows the Desktop shell locale. On macOS, Hide, Hide Others, Show All, and Quit use localized labels; Hide and Quit include the DeepSeek Harness product name. These commands retain their native actions and shortcuts. macOS reads the icon from its application bundle, so an unpackaged development launch displays Electron's icon; Windows receives the packaged PNG. Desktop’s local native directory flow opens an Electron folder dialog attached to the application window, restoring, showing, and focusing that window first. Concurrent requests share one dialog; cancellation returns no path and failures remain retryable. Ordinary Web uses the Host chooser. Browse mode lists Host directories. On Linux without zenity or kdialog, automatic selection uses browse instead of the Electron dialog. Desktop ships one pnpm distribution at `resources/runtime/primary-runtime/dependencies/pnpm`, without the native packages of other targets. Build-time production installation, the installed `dsh` CLI, Creator and the Web Plugin Manager execute its `bin/pnpm.mjs` with Electron Node mode; package operations do not require pnpm on PATH. The private Node launcher environment applies only to package operations. Agent workspace dependencies copy the same self-contained primary-runtime payload into the Harness home and execute pnpm with its standalone Node. Embedded Platform documents use a persistent WebContentsView partition keyed by a hash of the Platform origin and stable account ID. localStorage preferences, including dismissed notices, survive view closure and application restart; different accounts and origins use separate storage. The Host supplies the account ID from its latest successful profile read; while no ID is known, the document opens in a disposable partition that keeps no preference across opens. Opening a persistent partition clears cookies, filesystem, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, the HTTP and shader caches, service workers, and HTTP authentication before the document loads; a disposable partition clears all of its storage. Closing a view destroys the document, removes its request interceptors, and schedules the same cleanup, so authentication left by an unclean exit is cleared before the next document loads. The next open and application shutdown await that cleanup, and an update install waits for it before the installer takes over the exit. A failed cleanup rejects that open and blocks the same account until a later cleanup succeeds; other accounts keep opening. Sign-out destroys the document but retains account-scoped preferences for the next sign-in. A document already open in a disposable partition stays mounted when the account ID arrives for the same credential; the next open uses the account-scoped partition. The [storage decision](../../.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-09-22-platform-browser-storage.md) describes the retention policy. Host sends account credentials through private Node IPC; account RPC and the Harness renderer receive no token. Before page scripts execute, the Platform preload performs one synchronous IPC to read the prepared main-process credential. It exposes displayMode, synchronous getAuthToken() and getLocale() getters, and onLocaleChange(listener), which returns an unsubscribe function. Both getters read preload memory without further IPC. The bootstrap includes the resolved Desktop language (`zh_CN` or `en_US`); Settings language changes update the preload cache and notify the open Platform document without reloading. Platform applies this language before its first render and does not persist it as a browser preference. The main-process handler performs only sender validation and an in-memory read; it never waits for Host, disk, or network. Trusted-page initialization failures retain embedded mode and make the getter throw, preventing browser-credential fallback. Only the owned Platform main frame on the configured issuer origin can initialize. Sign-out, credential replacement, Host shutdown, and view closure destroy the document. Cross-origin document navigation is blocked. HTTPS links requesting a new window open in the system browser without the embedded session or token; other schemes and URL credentials are rejected. Native views occupy the viewport below the Account feature’s return bar. Desktop Host Platform API requests and update-policy requests identify the installed client with the same Platform client headers: platform, client version, locale, timezone offset in seconds, and a bundle id that is intentionally empty. Account operations take the calling UI's identity per call; the account provider owns [API-only header configuration](../../packages/credentials/deepseek-account-platform/README.md#use-this-package). Update policy additionally reports architecture, update channel, and bundled runtime version. The native account-state decoder accepts `no-response` sign-in failures and preserves the error code in the UI-safe projection. A server-expired account credential returns to Welcome when no official API key is configured; an available API key keeps the workspace open. Explicit sign-out follows the same rule. Both Welcome and the workspace display the localized expiry notice. Desktop microphone access is restricted to audio requests from the primary `dsh-app://app` frame. macOS uses system microphone authorization, a packaged usage description, and `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` in the main application and Helper signatures.

Experimental providers supply browser tools and manage each Session's browser resources. ## Table of Contents - [Packages](#packages) - [Related documentation](#related-documentation) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Packages Choose one provider and mount the shared registration service. | Package | Role | ctx key | |---|---|---| | [`browser-use`](browser-use/README.md) | Exclusive named provider registration | `ctx.browserUse` | ## Related documentation - [Browser use](../../docs/subsystems/browser-use.md) — capability ownership and provider choices. - [Experimental packages](../experimental/README.md) — Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, and Stagehand providers. ## Dev Note None.

--- description: "Computer-use capability packages for selecting and registering one desktop provider." kind: "package-group" --- # packages/computer-use English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary Computer-use providers let models observe and operate a desktop. This group contains the shared registry that prevents multiple providers from being enabled in one composition. DSH's [CUA implementation](../experimental/cua/README.md), platform providers, and opt-in bundle currently live in `experimental`, alongside the Cua Driver adapters. The CUA package documents the platform requirements for promotion to this group. ## Table of Contents - [Packages](#packages) - [Related documentation](#related-documentation) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Packages Choose one provider and mount the shared registration service. | Package | Role | ctx key | |---|---|---| | [`computer-use`](computer-use/README.md) | Exclusive named provider registration | `ctx.computerUse` | ## Related documentation - [Computer use](../../docs/subsystems/computer-use.md) — capability ownership and provider choices. - [Computer Use bundle](../experimental/cua-bundle/README.md) — enable native CUA and access its permission controls. - [Experimental packages](../experimental/README.md) — native CUA packages and Cua Driver adapters. ## Dev Note None.

--- description: "Inspect and operate native macOS applications through scoped app and window objects." kind: "package-reference" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-cua-macos English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary Inspect macOS permissions, select running applications and windows, read accessibility trees, capture screenshots and send input. The object API can be retained by an external persistent execution environment. The Swift helper uses macOS frameworks directly and adapts selected MIT-licensed Cua Driver behavior. This package owns neither a PTC runtime nor variable persistence. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) The helper supplies bounded 64-pixel PNG application icons for permission prompts and saved-application lists. Icon reads do not launch an application or inspect its windows; icons do not determine reusable consent. The helper runs through LaunchServices as an independent application: `DSH Computer Use.app` for release builds and `DSH Computer Use Dev.app` for source builds. Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions belong to this application. Permission guidance uses the responsible application’s bundle URL, identifier, filename, and system icon captured at startup; unavailable system attribution falls back to the independent helper’s own bundle. Dragging and Finder selection read the current on-disk bundle identifier and executable through the application-discovery reader. The page and guide both display the application’s `.app` filename. Existing connections retain their running application generation when another build updates `current.json`. When bundled inside another `.app`, it starts from a verified standalone copy; see [application storage](native/README.md#build-and-service). Permission requests open the selected privacy pane and a native floating guide. The guide selects the largest settings window once and follows that window by ID. It uses the normal window level, ordered immediately above the selected window so authentication dialogs remain above it. Placement reads window bounds without requesting Accessibility access. The guide stays hidden until the settings window is identified; a failed settings-open request displays manual navigation instructions independently. A material alpha mask gives the panel and its shadow rounded corners. The latest request replaces the shared guide, and only its owning connection can close it during cleanup. Navigation is attempted even when the application is unavailable, and the page reports that failure. Already-granted permissions open settings without a guide; explicit settings navigation dismisses previous guidance. A rejected settings-open request reports `SETTINGS_UNAVAILABLE`; missing or replaced application targets report `APPLICATION_UNAVAILABLE`. System Settings owns drag acceptance and any relaunch requirement. The provider resolves guide and recovery copy from the current Client language, with English for unsupported languages. Drag the guide’s application row into the permission list and enable its switch; enable the existing entry when already listed. The guide hides during dragging, closes when a drop is accepted, and returns after a canceled or rejected drag. The back button closes it and returns to the previous application. Right-click the row, or click it for keyboard focus and press Return or Space, to reveal the bundle in Finder. While open, the guide checks permission and window position every `permissionPollIntervalMs` (default 1000 ms), and closes after a confirmed grant, dismissal, disappearance of the settings window, or its owning connection’s cleanup. Dragging does not establish consent. Follow any macOS quit-and-reopen prompt; the shared helper is not automatically terminated. ----- ## Use this package This package is an optional macOS dependency. For local development, run `pnpm --dir packages/experimental/cua-macos run build:native` to generate an ad-hoc-signed application and `current.json` under `native/bin`. Release packaging requires `--identity "Developer ID Application: ()"` and notarization; see [native build and service](native/README.md#build-and-service). Installed packages preserve the distributed signature. A package inside an Electron `app.asar` archive reads its application from the sibling `app.asar.unpacked` directory, which the Desktop installer populates; an installed package without the application fails preparation with an error naming the expected directory. Source preparation requires Swift and Python 3 from Apple Command Line Tools. For repository Web use, enable [Computer Use](../cua-bundle/README.md) in Plugins. This prepares the local executable on macOS 14 or later; Windows support is in development. Subsequent builds check it while the existing Web profile keeps the bundle selected. Disabled profiles do not prepare native components. Explicit source composition is also available: ```sh pnpm dsh headless --patch packages/experimental/cua-macos/examples/macos.cordis.yml --dump-config ``` The dump command checks profile composition without a model request. For a real task, replace `--dump-config` with a prompt and configure the profile’s model credentials. The overlay mounts the computer-use registry and this provider; remove an existing competing provider before using it. The helper needs Accessibility permission for AX/input and Screen Recording permission for capture; use the Computer Use permission page to open System Settings and add the helper. Source builds use the bundle filename `DSH Computer Use Dev.app` and declare `DSH Computer Use Dev` in Info.plist; select the development entry when granting access. `getCapabilities` reports permissions and session lock state without opening a system dialog. Locked or unavailable desktop sessions reject UI observations and input before dispatch; the user must unlock macOS before resuming. `listApps` and `cua.getState` list running applications. `findApps(query)` searches standard macOS application directories by name, bundle ID or absolute path. `getApp` selects a unique name, bundle ID, path or running PID, obtains application consent, and launches a stopped app in the background when needed. A stopped application’s bundle identifier and executable path are read from disk before approval and rechecked before and after launch; applications without a bundle identifier use their canonical executable path for reusable consent. Selecting a stopped installation requests a new instance of that copy. The helper waits for the launched application to finish launching before returning its PID. A post-launch verification failure expires the pending handle but can leave the process running; inspect running applications before selecting a fresh handle. The returned object reads initial AX without activating the app. Launch cancellation may leave the application running. Model guidance starts with background observation and input, without activation during initialization or before each action. For hidden or minimized windows, try `app.show()` or `window.show()` and read fresh state. This requests unhide and unminimize without activation, raising or switching Spaces; app-level restoration selects the focused, main or sole AX window. The result names the selected `windowId`, or null when no window was selected, and reports `foregroundChanged` by comparing the front app and top window before and after the request. Null means foreground evidence was unavailable; later focus changes remain possible. If restoration fails or the window remains unusable, explain the needed foreground step, call `app.activate()` or an observed window’s `raise` action, then observe again. Necessary foreground access takes priority over preserving focus. Applications may change focus after input; background delivery does not guarantee an undisturbed user session. Source builds default to `sourceSigning: ad-hoc`, without creating certificates or keychains. Changed binaries can require new permission grants. To reduce repeated grants during rebuilds and across worktrees, select an existing certificate and its absolute keychain path in the DSH home’s `cordis.patch.yml`; `cua` is the entry ID loading `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-cua-macos`: ```yaml - id: cua config: sourceSigning: identity: "" keychain: "/Users//.cua-macos-keys/dev/signing.keychain-db" ```

overview: --- description: "The subagent package group: the delegation seam, its in-process and out-of-process backends, and the model-facing delegation tools." kind: "package-group" --- # subagent/ — subagent capability family English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary The subagent package family lets an agent delegate a task to a child, continue the child's work, and discover every child it created. Choose a fresh in-process child for isolated work, a history-seeded in-process child when prior conversation matters, or an out-of-process child backed by ACP, Codex, Claude Code, or another Harness runtime. Model-facing tools also let agents message adjacent agents, interrupt work, and list child status. Each child remains visible to its parent whether it is running or stored; the package READMEs document provider-specific setup and limits. ## Table of Contents - [Packages](#packages) - [Related documentation](#related-documentation) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Packages | Package | Role | ctx key | |---|---|---| | [`subagent/`](subagent/README.md) | Defines the delegation service: provider registry, one-shot runs, continuable children, and discovery | `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-spawn-in-process/`](subagent-spawn-in-process/README.md) | Runs a fresh in-process child | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-fork-in-process/`](subagent-fork-in-process/README.md) | Runs an in-process child seeded from the parent's completed history | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-acp/`](subagent-acp/README.md) | Runs an out-of-process child over the Agent Client Protocol | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-codex/`](subagent-codex/README.md) | Runs a real Codex child through the official app-server protocol | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-claude-code/`](subagent-claude-code/README.md) | Runs a real Claude Code child through the official Agent SDK | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`subagent-dsh-sdk/`](subagent-dsh-sdk/README.md) | Runs an out-of-process Harness child through the TypeScript SDK | registers on `ctx.subagents` | | [`tool-subagent/`](tool-subagent/README.md) | Exposes delegation to the model | registers on `ctx.tools` | | [`tool-subagent-control/`](tool-subagent-control/README.md) | Exposes adjacent-agent messaging, interrupt, and listing to the model | registers on `ctx.tools` | ----- ## Related documentation - [Subagent subsystem](../../docs/subsystems/subagent.md) — the service contract, provider contract, and terminal result semantics. - [historical Subagent capability seam](../../.agents/notes/archived/feature/2026-06-21-subagent-capability-seam.md) — the design record for the delegation capability family. - [Continuable subagents](../../.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-28-continuable-subagent-conversations.md) — durable children that accept follow-up turns. - [tool-subagent-control README](tool-subagent-control/README.md) — the follow-up, interrupt, and listing surface. ## Dev Note None.

--- description: "Coordinate subagents through a durable shared task board in Team-enabled Sessions." kind: "package-reference" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-team English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary `dsh-agent-team` adds a durable shared task board to an existing subagent tree. Members use standard subagent tools to discover and contact one another. Team adds compare-and-set task ownership. Mount `dsh-tool-agent-team` for task tools. Members share one checkout. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Use this package New Sessions, including ordinary forks, default to Team mode off. See the [Session-mode upgrade guide](../../../docs/upgrade-guide/v0.2.1-rc.2/session-team-mode/guide.md). Select **Use Agent Teams** in the root Session’s model and reasoning menu. Turning it off hides Team tools and guidance from subsequent steps throughout the tree while retaining tasks and subagents. The saved selection survives restart; a historical task board without a saved selection remains enabled. Set `defaultEnabled: true` to enable new root Sessions, including ordinary forks, before their first model step. Initialization saves the selection as `team/mode`; a save failure rejects Agent creation. Existing selections take precedence, and resuming a Session never applies the default, including when no selection was saved. Descendants use their live root's mode. The [SDK configuration guide](../../../docs/user/guide/python-sdk.md#enable-team-mode) includes a ready-to-use patch; the standard bundle keeps this option off. Mode changes take effect without waiting for queued task mutations. Each mutation checks the current mode when it starts: an admitted operation finishes, while queued work is rejected if Team is still off when it starts. Enabling again permits subsequent operations. A failed save leaves an appended selection active; retrying the same selection saves without another mode record. Add this package when subagents need durable shared task ownership and dependencies. Mount it with `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-agent-team` for model tools. ### When to choose it Choose it when delegated agents must divide and track shared work. Plain subagents suffice when no shared board is needed. Team does not create isolated working directories, coordinate across processes, or automatically release task owners. ### Smallest working setup Mount both Team packages in a composition that already provides continuable subagents, their messaging tools, and durable session storage, such as a profile built on `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base`: ```yaml # smallest Team addition over a composition with continuable subagents - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-team' - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-agent-team' ``` For example, ask the model to start a subagent to review the diff and track its work on the task board. Configuration fields are optional and validated at startup: | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---|

overview: --- description: "The persisted same-session goal service for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging one durable completion objective per session." kind: "package-reference" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-goal English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary `dsh-goal` lets one long-running completion objective persist across turns, session resume, fork, and process restarts. Users and agents can create, edit, pause, resume, complete, block, or clear it; compare-and-set updates reject stale views. A configurable round cap (256 by default) bounds automatic continuation, and blocked goals retain a stable policy code with a human-readable explanation. The package stores goal state but does not schedule work, and continuation permission remains process-local rather than durable. Choose it for one objective spanning many turns; skip it for routine single-turn work or parallel objectives. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Use this package Mount `dsh-goal` whenever a session should remember one long-running completion objective across many turns and restarts. The package is a service: the model tools, the `/goal` command, and the continuation driver are separate packages that consume the same goal state, so mounting only this package stores and serves the goal without starting any work. ### When to use it A goal suits one long-running completion objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds — for example shipping a migration or fixing every failing documentation gate. Routine single-turn work should not create a goal. The service keeps at most one current goal per session: an unfinished goal must be edited, paused, resumed, blocked, or cleared before another takes its place, while a completed goal can be replaced directly. ### Set up the service Load the package with a composition entry; the only deployment choice is the default round cap applied to creates that do not name their own. ```yaml - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-goal' config: defaultMaxGoalRounds: 256 ``` | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `defaultMaxGoalRounds` | `256` | Round cap applied when a create request omits its own | `defaultMaxGoalRounds` must be a positive safe integer; a create request that names its own cap overrides it. The generated [configuration catalog](../../../docs/config-catalog.md#deepseek-aidsh-goal) is the exhaustive source for every accepted field. ### Session projection `GoalService` requires `ctx.sessionProjections` ([`@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-projection`](../../session/session-projection/README.md)) and registers the `goal` projection unit at startup; a composition that omits the projection registry cannot activate `ctx.goals`. The unit's version 6 host state retains the latest valid current goal, every previously used goal id, and the first strict replay failure. Its client view exposes the current goal or `null` before the first create and after a clear tombstone. The client key merges into `SessionProjectionMap`; carriers serve the client value on the history tail page and the `session/projection` push frame. ### Drive the lifecycle

overview: --- description: "Plan mode for users and maintainers choosing, configuring, or debugging the per-agent planning feature with deployment guidance, a /plan command, and a user-reviewed exit." kind: "package-reference" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-plan-mode English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary Plan mode asks an agent to explore and design before execution, then presents the finished plan for your approval. Enter it with `/plan`, optionally with a message or ordered image and file attachments; leave with `/plan off`, approve the review to continue, or return feedback for more planning. Deployment-defined guidance controls planning behavior, but every tool remains available, so use sandbox mode and approval prompts for enforced limits. The active state survives session resume and forks. Choose it when you want a reviewed plan before the agent acts. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Use this package When plan mode is active, the agent works under your instructions and presents its plan for review instead of executing right away. The common path: configure the guidance text, enter plan mode with `/plan`, and review the finished plan when the agent calls `exit_plan_mode`. ### When to choose it Choose plan mode when the agent should explore and design before executing and you want to approve the plan first. It does not restrict the agent: every tool stays callable, so use sandbox mode and approval prompts when you need enforced limits. Skip it when the agent should act on your requests immediately, without a planning phase. ### Minimal configuration The only required configuration is the guidance text the agent follows while planning; anything else you add fails at load. ```yaml - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-plan-mode' config: section: | You are in plan mode. Explore and design before presenting the complete plan through exit_plan_mode. ``` | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `section` | required | Guidance rendered as the `plan:policy` prompt section while plan mode is active | The generated [configuration catalog](../../../docs/config-catalog.md#deepseek-aidsh-plan-mode) is the exhaustive source for every accepted field and its JSDoc. ### Entering and leaving plan mode Type `/plan` to enter plan mode, or `/plan ` to enter with an instruction — the message becomes your next request under plan guidance. Type `/plan off` to leave plan mode directly; it also cancels a plan-mode entry that has not taken effect yet.

overview: --- description: "The model-facing web tools (web_search, web_fetch) over ctx.web: how deployments enable, configure, and observe the search and fetch tools the model sees." kind: "package-reference" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-web English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary `dsh-tool-web` lets models search the web with `web_search` and retrieve pages with `web_fetch`. Choose it when an agent needs current information or full source text, and enable either tool independently through package configuration. Results label provider-controlled text as external and untrusted, while fetched HTML excludes active and hidden content. If a configured provider is missing or unavailable, the tool remains visible and returns a structured error the model can act on; a request is not offered a tool whose operations the selected provider cannot authenticate. Timeout and result-size limits are deployment settings rather than model arguments. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Use this package Load the package in a composition that already mounts the web service and at least one search or fetch backend; it adds `web_search` and `web_fetch` to the model's toolset and their guidance to the system prompt. ### When to choose it Choose this package when the model should discover current information or read a specific page: `web_search` returns an optional answer plus source URLs, and `web_fetch` retrieves a page's content as text. A product that wants only one tool disables the other via config (`{ search: false }` or `{ fetch: false }`); search guidance mentions `web_fetch` only when fetch is also enabled, and a search-only composition instead tells the model to use returned snippets and cite their URLs. ### Minimal configuration Load the web service, at least one backend, and this package; both tools register by default. ```yaml - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-web' - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-deepseek-api' - name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-web' ``` | Field | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `search` | `true` | Register `web_search` | | `fetch` | `true` | Register `web_fetch` | | `searchMaxResults` | `10` | Upper bound on sources returned by one `web_search` call | | `searchMaxQueries` | `10` | Upper bound on queries accepted by one `web_search` call; the value appears in prompt guidance and schema descriptions | | `searchSummaryMaxChars` | `800` | Cap on each source summary in `web_search` output, in characters, including the `…` that marks a cut | | `fetchTimeoutMs` | `30000` | Cooperative tool-call timeout budget (ms) for `web_fetch` | | `searchTimeoutMs` | `30000` | Cooperative tool-call timeout budget (ms) for `web_search` | | `fetchMaxOutputChars` | `200000` | Cap on source characters converted synchronously and on one complete `web_fetch` output | The generated [configuration catalog](../../../docs/config-catalog.md#deepseek-aidsh-tool-web) is the exhaustive source for every accepted field and its JSDoc. `searchMaxQueries` bounds the accepted array before exact-string deduplication and provider fan-out; validation rejects an oversized array before any search starts. The timeout budgets attach to each tool definition and are enforced by [`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy`](../../guard/timeout-policy/README.md); the model-facing schemas expose no timeout argument.
